sources.excerpt: The simpler dioptric (purely refractive) form of the lens was first proposed by Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon, and independently reinvented by the French physicist Augustin-Jean Fresnel (1788–1827) for use in lighthouses.
Because of its use in lighthouses, it has been called "the invention that saved a million ships".
The Lighthouse of Alexandria, sometimes called the Pharos of Alexandria, was a lighthouse built by the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Ancient Egypt, during the reign of Ptolemy II Philadelphus (280–247 BC).
One of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, for many centuries it was one of the world's tallest man-made structures.

Once widely used, the number of operational lighthouses has declined due to the expense of maintenance and the advent of much cheaper, more sophisticated, and more effective electronic navigational systems.
Lighthouses mark dangerous coastlines, hazardous shoals, reefs, rocks, and safe entries to harbors; they also assist in aerial navigation.

A lighthouse is a tower, building, or other type of physical structure designed to emit light from a system of lamps and lenses and to serve as a beacon for navigational aid for maritime pilots at sea or on inland waterways.

editorNotes: Alternatives checked: a beacon or a buoy also warns shipping, but neither is a tower of lamps and lenses and neither was a Wonder of the Ancient World; a lightship floats rather than stands; the Fresnel lens itself is the fitting, not the structure the clues describe.
